articles.title: On getting to know your neighbors
articles.description: I have what I realize might be a Hollywood-induced pipe dream about knowing my neighbors. Wouldn't it be nice to knock on a door to borrow some eggs or ask how best to work the heater? Or on the bus to make conversation with the person next to you about the weather or sports or whatever else you talk about when you'll never see someone again? Instead we put our AirPods in as we're leaving home and don't take them out until we've reached our destination. We go out and buy new eggs if we need them or think twice about whatever we were planning on cooking. We figure out how to work the heater for ourselves. There are plenty of good reasons why we do things the way we do them. It's better in the long run to have a fully stocked fridge, and conversations had on public transportation have the potential to be rather unpleasant. Still, we're giving up the opportunity to meet people who live completely differently from us. A young family with kids or an older person who is settling down. Instead, we get all wrapped up inside our own little worlds. The bad grade we got on an exam feels even more world ending because we have no window into a world that isn't related to school. We find ourselves frequenting the same few places with the same few people because we forget that there are things to do we haven't tried yet and people we have yet to meet. Maybe everyone else knocks on their neighbors' doors with a plate of cookies when they first move in, and I'm just shy or lagging behind. I have seen no evidence of this, though. It's hard to be the one to sit on the JHMI without a phone in your hand or earbuds in your ears, but I've decided to try to do it. Most conversations may be short two-liners or downright flops, but even so, I'll be making my world a little bigger with each one and reminding myself that the world doesn't consist of the same few people I see day in and day out. Our culture doesn't lend itself to interacting with strangers, so many people aren't ready to think of it. I think I'll try a little though. Maybe nothing as involved as knocking on the neighbors' door out of the blue, but if you see me around, feel free to give me a wave. I'll do my best to say something dazzling about some aspect of our surroundings. Who knows what we may notice together when we break up our routine? Amelia Taylor is a junior from Potomac, Md. studying Writing Seminars and Voice Performance. In her column, she draws insights from seemingly random experiences that present themselves in the course of ordinary life.

articles.title: How to Survive Authoritarianism: A book talk
articles.description: On Oct. 12, 2026 the International Studies Program welcomed Hopkins alumni Dan Storyev and his co-author Maria Kuznetsova to converse about their book, How to Survive Authoritarianism: A Russian's Phrasebook for Everyday Life in America. Victoria Juharyan, director of the Russian Program in the Center for Language Education, moderated the discussion. Kuznetsova began the event by explaining that she came up with the book idea after seeing a shift in the American political state. She lived in Russian and other European countries, and she moved to the U.S. in 2023 to study at Harvard. "When Trump came back to power in 2025, I immediately noticed how the mood shifted… I started to get a lot of questions from my American friends of, like, what we can do, what is the most effective way to fight back… because they knew I was a dissident, and I worked for many years against Putin's regime in Moscow," Kuznetsova shared. Storyev added that he and Kuznetsova wrote an op-ed about six Russian terms for authoritarianism to help Americans describe current events. The Russian brand of authoritarianism has evolved through the Czars, Stalin and Brezhnev stagnation. In contrast, authoritarianism has been less common in American history, so Americans lack the language to fully describe these systems. Storyev focuses on America's political backsliding: a gradual, state-led decline in the quality of democracy into a more authoritarian mode of governance. "[Trump and his administration] are definitely borrowing either from Russia, Poland, Hungary or maybe also from Israel," said Kuznetsova. "There are a lot of specific elements that come from our regions… Trump is moving into the direction of tyranny much quicker than Putin did." This borrowing of ideology isn't one-directional. Just as American politicians have used strategies pioneered by other nations, other nations have used methods prevalent among Americans. For example, Putin borrowed American conservative ideologies about transgender people. Storyev claimed that the argument of the book is that the U.S. is entering a period of soft authoritarianism, or at the least, containing elements pointing towards a more authoritarian direction. Elizabeth Kesler, a sophomore at Hopkins, spoke about her worries about the prevalence of patterns of authoritarianism in an interview with The News-Letter. She described the importance of being able to recognize these patterns. "I think about different developments that are happening, and I'm uncomfortable with them," she said. "But I guess there's a lot of things that I wouldn't realize or notice are patterns of authoritarianism until I hear them." The authors also discussed the concept of survival over rebellion, and how existence itself could be seen as a form of fighting back. When in a regime that wants submission, the actual act of continuing to exist when they would want all discontented civilians to be gone, can be a tactic of rebellion. Storyev emphasizes that oppression creates mental health and substance abuse issues. Storyev believes that the combination of internal instability and external instability can lead to revolutions. "When [people] end up actually winning and seizing power, they might end up replicating the authoritarian system that they fought against, or even creating one that is inexplicably worse than the one they destroyed," said Stroyev. "You can survive authoritarianism by opting out of the resistance." How to Survive Authoritarianism is rooted in a Russian humorist tradition, Aesopian speech, because explicitly mentioning events would exile writers to Siberia for punishment, and using analogies to describe political events was safer. The authors described these more subtle acts of rebellion as being safer and more effective. For example, as seen throughout historical rebellions, some factory workers will purposefully make faulty equipment to sabotage production of weaponry. In a government where actions are very controlled, it is important to recognize that just because major actions cannot be taken by every person, there are ways to combat it regardless. "They didn't quit their job" Kuznetsova said. "But they just made sure that everything they produced just doesn't work." When addressing a changing society, one of the authors' main points was understanding the language changes. In Russia, there are a variety of words and phrases that emerge during periods of oppression or authoritarianism. These sayings may be used to describe common occurrences, but they are specific products of authoritarian influence. For example, there is the Russian saying: "держать фигу в кармане." Storyev explained how this phrase would translate to English and what it means. "It's essentially living your life with a middle finger in your pocket," he said. This means that people can do very small things to resist the government and make it harder for authoritarian regimes to persist while living normally and avoiding conviction. Some language also describes the people who take more direct methods of resistance: fighting back without getting caught. For example, creating "suspicious fires" and burning drafting offices was a way to rebel against unfair enlistment. These buildings would "mysteriously" catch on fire as a form of rebellion. Storyev joked that many people would say that "somebody was smoking" nearby. This saying is used fires even when referring to something other than the burning of draft offices. This shift in language reveals how a society might be changing too. If these sayings or terms are needed, it can be a sign that a country itself is shifting to a similar regime to Russia's. Furthermore, Storyev introduced the Russian phrase "Моя хата с краю, ничего не знаю," an example of a Russian authoritarianism phrase with no direct English translation. "[It means] my house is at the very edge of the township, and therefore I don't care whatever is happening to the rest of the township, right? And so that's sort of the attitude that authoritarian regimes try to engender, and then there is the other one, inner immigration," he explains. When phrases start appearing within the government, too, this can be an alarming sign of change. Storyev then connected these language shifts to new patterns in American politics. In leaked Depart of Defense memos, "near abroad" was used a few times to describe parts of the Soviet Union in a discreet way. "There are very visible, literally vocabulary shifts in the way [the] Trump administration is talking about politics," Storyev stated. "Near abroad is how the Kremlin refers to the former Soviet states, so the states which it sees as within its sphere of influence… They are learning from one another, and they are teaching one another." In addition, the phrase "enemy of the people" has been used by Trump, which was a phrase similarly used by Stalin. Kuznetsova described how Trump used the phrase to address different American and non-American entities. "Trump started to use, even during his first term, the term "the enemy of the people" as a reference to [the] press," she said. Though not yet used in the U.S., other terms like "political technologists" describe people who engineer government while keeping it under a professional facade. Watching for these borrowed language changes can be a way to detect authoritarian leaning shifts earlier on. Misha Zhernevskii, a sophomore at Hopkins, shared how his Russian identity and knowledge of the Russian language shaped his experience at the event in an interview with The News-Letter. He was specifically surprised by the linguistics differences between English and common Russian phrases he used to use. "I would say I definitely didn't realize that some concepts - I was familiar with all of these words - have either [a] weak connection or like no representation in the English language," he explained. "Because everybody understands [the concepts], I would just like to think like, 'Oh yeah, that's just, like, the way things work.' I didn't realize it was [the] heritage of [the] Soviet machine." Another part of the event was spent comparing authoritarianism and democracy, and how while the loss of individual rights through authoritarianism is looked down upon, there are positives that can be drawn from it, partly showing why that form of government is able to last. In cities like Moscow and Shanghai, the intense surveillance and facial recognition reduces crime significantly. Specifically, the safety of women is prioritized. "As a woman, I was so much safer in Moscow than like in any American city," Kuznetsova explained. "[Because] people know that there are so many cameras, people just don't commit so much crime, especially on the streets because, like, you know what's gonna happen." However, in Moscow, that same facial recognition software is used to detain activists who are protesting. Kuznetsova herself has personal experience with this. "I was detained in Moscow multiple times using facial recognition in [the] metro and on protest because I'm in some activist database, not because I committed some crime," she said. An app called Gosuslugi allows people to perform a ton of everyday tasks on one app, but the trade-off is that all of their information is taken. Storyev describes the app as being used to sign kids up for school, complete government documents, pay taxes, register to vote and make a doctor's appointment. However, he also explained the consequences of having a streamlined app. "The same app is being used to send people draft notices to go and fight in Ukraine, and the same app is being used to find people who were spotted at protests," Storyev said. This kind of technological advantage is present in other parts of people's lives. "Paying with your face" is a common practice in Russia, where someone can scan their face and their bank data is already accessible, allowing them to pay without a phone or card. Delivery robots are common, and while there has been backlash in the U.S. on the same concept, it is widely accepted in Russia. There is a large stress put on data mismanagement by companies like Google and Facebook in the U.S., but in Russia, many people just fear how their data could lead to detention or arrest. The main trade-off is efficiency with personal privacy. While the logic of "no wrongdoing" can be considered an easy way to survive government scrutiny, it becomes easy to target anyone out of line when you are constantly monitored. As a government progresses, these behaviors become more normalized, explaining why Russian citizens tend to have a warmer opinion toward technological integration even at the expense of personal freedom. A common misconception addressed by both authors was how capitalism can lead to political freedom. Being able to run your own businesses, grow in the economy and not being limited in your financial independence is often tied to a "freer" government like democracy. While it is true that a standard capitalist state has labor rights and opposition when needed, checks and balances and regulations, these factors are not necessary for capitalism to exist. A country could have private businesses, investments and markets without these rights. Monitoring would be higher, but authoritarianism can coincide with it. According to Storyev, some capitalists may even prefer authoritarianism, as it allows them to prevent labor unions and opposition. "Capitalism works great under an authoritarian regime because you can really squeeze everything out of people, right? There is no labor rights to be worried about," Storyev explained. In this regard, he warned not to tie democracy and capitalism together, claiming that "democracy does not equal capitalism" and that just because capitalism persists, it doesn't mean our society isn't veering toward a different form of government.

articles.title: Martian Polar Crater Ice Shifts with Seasonal Frost
articles.description: The planet Mars shares many landforms and weather patterns with the Earth, including changing seasons, volcanoes, canyons, dust storms and dust devils, and water ice. But one feature that Earth and Mars share among the eight planets in our solar system are polar ice caps. Both are one of each planet’s striking features, but the major difference is while Earth’s polar ice caps are both comprised of water, Mars’ north polar ice cap is only comprised of water while its southern polar ice cap is carbon dioxide. The reasons for this are determined by altitude, but Mars’ northern polar ice cap is one of the most studied regions primarily due to its water ice composition. But how does the north polar ice cap water ice change with the seasons compared to Earth, and what can this teach scientists about Mars’ climate history?

articles.title: This oddball reflective lava world is challenging to understand
articles.description: Among Kepler and TESS's many surprising exoplanet discoveries are the ultra-short-period (USP) planets. These planets move very quickly and complete an orbit in less than 24 hours. Ancient astronomers thought that Mercury was so fast—it goes around the sun every 88 days—that they named it after the Roman god Mercury, who was the fast-traveling messenger of the gods. They couldn't have known how sluggish Mercury is compared to the USPs.

articles.title: Ceres' Water Ice Can Mask Massive Surface Salt Deposits
articles.description: The dwarf planet Ceres is arguably one of the most overlooked and underappreciated planetary objects in the entire solar system. This could be because while Ceres has the same dwarf planet designation as Pluto, Ceres is largely considered an “asteroid” since it resides the in main asteroid belt. However, along with being the largest object in the main asteroid belt, Ceres’ mass comprises between 25 to 30 percent of all the mass of the entire main asteroid belt. Despite its lack of recognition, Ceres’ interior is layered like most rocky planets, including Pluto, and its surface displays evidence of past water ice activity (also called cryovolcanism) with several “bright spots”, which are highly reflective salt deposits. But what can these salt deposits teach scientists about Ceres’ formation and evolution?

articles.title: Computer Simulations Suggest Building Blocks of Life Didn't Arrive on Prehistoric Comets
articles.description: CNN reports: The popular theory that comets were crucial in kick-starting life on Earth billions of years ago may not hold up, according to new computer simulations that counter decades of scientific thinking. The finding suggests the fragile organic molecules supposedly carried by the icy objects would have been destroyed on impact, upending an established origin of life theory that dates back to at least 1961 [with earlier versions postulated in 1908]... Early in its history — over 4 billion years ago — Earth may have experienced a period of heavy bombardment from more than 100,000 comets larger than 100 meters (328 feet), according to the new study, published Wednesday in the journal Scientific Reports. Those impacts, however, were mostly too heavy for life-starting molecules to withstand. The team used the latest models of comet formation and evolution to simulate this early planetary period 100,000 times. "Given what we know about surface environments on the early Earth, on average, our simulations found that there were no successful impacts," said lead study author Richard Anslow, who conducted the research while completing his doctorate at the Institute of Astronomy of the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom... "The typical velocities of these comets when they impact the Earth meant that actually very few, if any, would have been able to deliver intact organic molecules, so comets actually don't seem to be as useful for prebiotic chemistry as was previously thought," Anslow said. More precisely, 54% of the simulations showed no impact at all, while the remaining 46% had at least one and a "tiny minority" returned up to three collisions, Anslow said. "We can't rule out confidently that there was never a successful impact — there could have been one of these fluke impacts." However, such flukes had to occur in a "perfect location" that already met several important conditions, including the presence of liquid water and other chemicals needed to support life. That combination makes the overall process unlikely, he added. The article notes his argument that even if a successful impact occurred, it's unlikely an important chemical like hydrogen cyanide (HCN) could survive the impact, and would've dissolved in an ocean impact. Plus, "many other precursor molecules are also needed, such as compounds that contain phosphorus and sulfur, but these are not routinely found in comets, Anslow said." An alternative cosmic source of organic material could have been asteroids, which typically struck Earth more slowly and in greater numbers. Anslow pointed to recent findings on samples from asteroids Bennu and Ryugu, which contain the majority of protein-building amino acids. The recent study also raises another intriguing possibility: While Earth may not have had the ideal conditions to foster HCN from comet impacts, ancient Mars might have been better suited. "Because Mars is much smaller than Earth and further away from the sun, the typical impact velocity of comets is much lower, so while these impacts on Earth were destroying most of the HCN, this wasn't the case so much for Mars," Anslow said. This idea could add another dimension to the long-standing question of whether the red planet once supported life. While the authors closely analyzed how HCN could have survived comet impact, the chemical may have undergone reactions before the icy bodies entered Earth's atmosphere, said Queenie Chan, an associate professor of Earth sciences at Royal Holloway University of London, who was not involved with the study. This process could have created biologically important compounds, such as those protein building blocks, that are less volatile and more likely to survive. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Cardi B to headline the rescheduled 2026 Hoptoberfest, Take Back the Night rally also rescheduled
articles.description: On Saturday, Oct. 31 at 1:30 p.m., the Hopkins Student Organization for Programming (HOP) and the Leadership Engagement and Experiential Development (LEED) office released an update regarding the annual Hoptoberfest Concert. The concert has been moved to 8 p.m. on Sunday, Nov. 1. An email sent from the HOP and LEED to ticket holders described the additional change to the concert, announcing that Cardi B will be the new headliner. "Due to unforeseen circumstances, Daniel Cesar is no longer able to perform," the email read. "However, we are excited to announce that our new headliner is none other than…CARDI B!!!" The concert had initially been scheduled for Saturday at 8 p.m., with Daniel Caesar announced as the concert's headliner on Monday Oct. 19. Ticket sales were supposed to go live at 12 PM on Wednesday Oct. 21 but were delayed until 7 p.m., where they were sold out by the end of the day. Hundreds of people remain on the waitlist. Belcalis Marlenis Almánzar, known by her stage name Cardi B, is an American rapper who is best known for her songs "Bodak Yellow," "WAP" feat. Megan Thee Stallion and "I Like It" with Bad Bunny and J Balvin. Cardi B released her newest album, "Am I the Drama," in Sept. 2025 and has embarked on the Little Miss Drama Tour earlier this year, performing at Baltimore's CFG Bank Arena in April. She is the first female rapper to have won the Grammy Award for Best Rap Album in 2019 for her 2018 album "Invasion of Privacy," in addition to numerous other accolades. Students who obtained tickets for the concert through the original ticket sale will retain their tickets for the new artist and the new time. The concert will still be hosted in the Ralph S. O'Connor Center for Recreation & Well-Being. In an interview with The News-Letter, sophomore Bhavya Guru expressed her excitement about the change, despite the previous Saturday date working better for her schedule and being a fan of Daniel Caesar. "I was actually pretty excited about Daniel Caesar, I do listen to a good amount of his music," she said. "When they switched it to Cardi B, I was a little surprised and honestly thought it was fake. I'm honestly really hyped for Cardi B and think it's going to be a lot of fun. I feel like it's going to be really good to hear a lot of throwbacks." In an interview with The News-Letter, sophomore Lana Hakma said that the date change to Sunday works better for her schedule and explained that she is more familiar with the new artist. "I am personally really excited about the change," she said. "I like Cardi B a lot better and I know her songs." Hoptoberfest is typically held on Saturdays, not Sundays, due to its time and morning classes held on Mondays. This year, an additional conflict has arisen. Hopkins students were planning to host a National Campus Take Back the Night (TBTN) rally at 8 p.m on Sunday, the exact new time of the concert. A few hours after the announcement, the Instagram page of the rally organizers has updated the new time of the rally to be 4 p.m. on Sunday, Nov. 1. "After weeks of organizing and coordinating with the university, learning of this change just one day before our event is deeply disheartening," the organizers wrote in the account's Instagram story. The (TBTN) rally is intended to be a moment where each campus community can come together to show solidarity for survivors of sexual and gender-based violence. On each campus, there will be speakers and an optional march through campus. The keynote speaker for the Hopkins rally will be Renee Williams, the CEO of the National Center for Victims of Crime. The event is posted for registration on Hopkins Groups and currently has nine registered attendees. The event includes a brief blurb about the event and its history. "In light of the recent news from Cornell University, a national rally will be held at college campuses on November 1," it reads "Toke [sic] Back The Night started in 1973, when women at the University of South Florida put on black sheets, picked up broomsticks, and marched across campus to demand a women's center. It is the world's oldest movement against sexual violence." The News-Letter has reached out to HOP and the rally's organizers about the scheduling conflict. Both parties have not yet replied for comment. Grace Oh contributed to the reporting of this article.

articles.title: When Electric Cars Were for Women
articles.description: At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000. For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place. Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with. Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations. A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it. Who Invented the Mercury-Arc Rectifier? Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps. The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery. A Carriage Maker Pivots to Electric Cars I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass. According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago. Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles. Thomas Edison Designed a Bad Battery Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market. While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5). Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling. When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular. Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.) Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles. Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today. Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology. An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue. References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine. Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

articles.title: Rare fossil discovery reveals new dinosaur species that specialized in eating fruit
articles.description: Among the ravenous carnivores and lumbering herbivores that roamed the Cretaceous landscape, another kind of dinosaur was evolving that started to eat something else: the plants that began to flower and produce fruit. The discovery by paleontologists from Stony Brook University, Royal Ontario Museum (ROM) and the North Dakota Geological Survey reveals that a new species, Infernogallus jamesi—a type of small oviraptorosaur—had chewing muscles for mashing soft food, making it the first known dinosaur that specifically ate fruit.

articles.title: Bodian Seminar: Translating sensations to perceptions across species
articles.description: How do you know to stretch out your left hand to catch a ball thrown at you from the left? How do you know where to look when you hear a sound coming from behind you? Somewhere between the light entering your eyes or the sound entering your ears, your brain has to turn that collection of sensory signals into something meaningful. In a Bodian Seminar hosted by the Zanvyl Krieger Mind/Brain Institute on Oct. 19, guest speaker Madineh Sedigh-Sarvestani focused on answering these exact questions. Sedigh-Sarvestani is an Assistant Professor of Neurobiology & Behaviour at Cornell University, and her lab focuses on understanding how our brains and bodies translate sensation into perception. At the center of her research is the idea of a "sensory-motor dictionary." "Our core hypothesis is that sensation doesn't come pre-labeled with meaning," Sedigh-Sarvestani explained. The idea is that movements of the body produce predictable changes in sensory information. Over time, the brain learns these relationships and uses them to understand the world. "The dictionary is rooted in body movements," she said. One example of the distinction between sensation and perception comes from adults who undergo cataract-removal surgery after many years of limited vision. Following a successful surgery, patients can immediately detect light and other visual information, but they may need weeks to recognize familiar people and objects. The theory of the sensory-motor dictionary led Sedigh-Sarvestani to an unusual species: treeshrews. Treeshrews have eyes positioned on the side of their heads, similar to mice and rats. Based on this eye placement, researchers expect to see tree shrews relying on head movements rather than eye movements to shift their gaze. Primates, by comparison, can move their eyes independently of their heads to change what they're looking at. Sedigh-Sarvestani's research demonstrates that treeshrews may occupy an unusual position between these two groups. Studying just the pupils of head-fixed treeshrews; she observed that they were able to make small, five-degree eye movements, 90% of which were without any head movement at all. "Much of their visual system seems specialized for sampling the binocular field in front of them," Sedigh-Sarvestani said. But why? A treeshrew doesn't need to look at an iPhone or interpret facial expressions. Their highly specialized vision frontal is surprising for a small, nonsocial animal. Sedigh-Sarvestani hypothesized that the animal's unique ability to control their visual system comes from their body movements. During the seminar, Sedigh-Sarvestani showed footage of a treeshrew in her lab leaping between branches in its enclosure, and executing an almost 180 degree rotation in the air to easily land on the next branch. A treeshrew jumping between branches may need to move its head and body in one direction while keeping its eyes oriented toward a landing point. Independent eye movements could allow the animal to maintain useful visual information even while its body is rotating through space. To test whether motor information actually contributes to perception, the lab changed the relationship between movement and visual input. In one experiment, tree shrews were trained to move their gaze toward a visual target. Researchers then reversed the relationship between eye movement and the target's movement, so that moving their eyes in one direction caused the target to move in the opposite direction. The animals were able to adapt to the new relationship within a matter of weeks. Sedigh-Sarvestani is pursuing this question further through experiments involving treeshrew-sized goggles with inverting prisms. The specially designed goggles make the animals' visual world appear upside down, forcing them to adapt to a fundamentally different relationship between their movements and what they see. This is an experiment that can easily be done on humans - many students may even encounter a version in their introductory psychology classes - but it can be very difficult to execute on animals. As Sedigh-Sarvestani put it, "[Tree shrews] are highly mobile, and their movements require vision." Thus, they are good candidates for this style of experiment. The animals initially struggled to navigate the altered environment. They hesitated to execute their previous amazing acrobatic jumps. Over time, however, they began to adjust their movements and eventually regained the ability to perform complex behaviors such as jumping between branches. If visual neurons change their responses as an animal learns a new relationship between movement and vision, such as completely flipping the visual field upside down, it would suggest that perception is not based solely on what reaches the retina. Instead, the brain may incorporate information about the body's movements to determine what those sensory signals mean. For Sedigh-Sarvestani, understanding this relationship could provide a new way of thinking about perception itself. Rather than passively receiving information from the world, the brain may constantly learn what its sensations mean through the body's interactions with its environment. The ability to catch a ball, navigate a branch or simply recognize an object may therefore depend on a sensory-motor dictionary that the brain has spent a lifetime learning to read.

articles.title: Wherever you go, there you are!
articles.description: It's been a little over a month since I started college, but I continue to find myself trapped in the cycle of meeting new people and then confronting the inevitable small talk. I am aware I should be grateful to still be meeting new, kind, and interesting people - and I am! - but I thoroughly dread the perplexing question that invariably follows: Where are you from? I've reached a monotonous state in which I simply answer Seattle. I actually live in the suburbs (sue me), but if I say Washington, chances are the freshman will eagerly ask, "D.C.?" and then I am forced to quash the exciting prospect of me being a local tour guide with the anticlimactic clarification of Washington State. This is admittedly not a big deal. But I, too, am an exhausted freshman at Hopkins and, in the interest of optimizing my time and preserving my sanity, do not wish to divulge my entire life story to this person in my 200-person lecture hall whom I may or may not ever see again. At least take me out to dinner first! But it is important to be sociable, and I actually am a caring person, so the conversation usually continues. They ask me a follow up question about Grey's Anatomy and Seattle, and suddenly my story begins to unravel. "Well, actually, I've only lived in Seattle for two years" "Oh, so where are you really from?" No! Now I am trapped sharing my life story. Well, before that, I lived in Florida for a while. But I hated Florida. I feel compelled to make this distinction known. Perhaps I am being pretentious, unwilling to be associated with "Florida man" and all that transpires down there, but I cannot help myself. I usually explain I hated the heat, which is entirely true. The only thing I loathe more than this conversation is the humidity in Baltimore. "But are you from there?" No. Well, actually, I was born in Beijing and lived there for six years until my parents decided to move back to the U.S., eventually settling in Florida. It was cheaper, okay? Now I am presumably asked why my parents moved there, to which I have no answer. And don't get me wrong: I absolutely loved Beijing. It was my first home, and I cherish the culture and everything it imparted on me. But it feels slightly presumptuous for me, a white girl, to claim that I understand that experience when, in this particular moment, I only receive the favorable end of it. That is - an interesting conversation starter. Now I am stuck feeling as though this conversation, in which we are supposedly getting to know each other, has become entirely centered upon me and my life, when you were probably just being polite. You did not ask for the synopsis of my existence. And maybe, selfishly, I am writing this very article in the hopes that people read it and not have to ask me this question. This brings me to my final qualm: what does "where are you from?" even mean? I am privileged in that I do not have to deal with people looking condescendingly as they ask someone where they are "originally" from. But I would like to think I am not alone in this confusion. The question itself seems woefully underspecified. What if we collectively agreed to ask, "Where did you last live?" But, to play devil's advocate - and put my philosophical hat on - am I the problem with today's society? We are all so focused on achieving our next goal and optimizing every spare moment that a simple question, one that could potentially lead to more conversation, becomes dreadful. And is that not the very essence of communication? That those small, even awkward moments, can lead to lasting connections? That an unassuming question can reveal something far more substantial? Or perhaps I am putting too much pressure on this interaction in its entirety. Maybe no one cares what I am answering, nor are they listening with the attention that I am imagining. Maybe they, too, are simply hoping to move on with their day. Ultimately, though, I can fall into existentialism. What even is the act of "from" somewhere? What does telling you where I am from actually reveal about me? Oftentimes, our living situations are merely circumstantial. Maybe the fact that I have moved fairly frequently tells you I am trying to escape myself. Or maybe my parents were in the military. They were not. I suppose this is the point of small talk. The question itself is not necessarily meant to produce a meaningful answer; it is intended to open the door to a new bond. Perhaps the places we come from do matter. Of course, our environments shape our formative years and influence the people we ultimately become. But if we are talking about the one-word answer of a city or county, does that really tell me much about you? I propose an amendment. I think this question is inherently flawed. What if we asked, "Where are you going?" Then you can tell me about where you are from if it serves a relevant purpose or if you so please. But I personally would much rather hear about your aspirations or what excites you, as that makes you, you. As they say: "Wherever you go, there you are!" Mirabelle DeAngelis is a freshman from Bellevue, Wash. majoring in Applied Mathematics and Statistics.
